toEnglish.explanation: ausmachen is macht … aus (puts out) glued back together at the end of the weil clause, with the plural ending -en for die Kinder; then the main verb weint jumps straight after the comma, ahead of its subject die Hexe.

toLang.prompt: When the witch sleeps, the children put out the fire.
accepted: Wenn die Hexe schläft, machen die Kinder das Feuer aus.
Die Kinder machen das Feuer aus, wenn die Hexe schläft.
Wenn die Hexe schläft, löschen die Kinder das Feuer.
Die Kinder löschen das Feuer, wenn die Hexe schläft.
toLang.explanation: After a fronted wenn clause the main verb comes first, right after the comma (machen, plural for die Kinder), then the subject; and because this is a main clause the particle aus still splits off to the very end.

grammar: Particles that make machen mean open, close, light, put out. The meaning of the verb really sits in the particle.
In a main clause the particle splits off and goes to the very end.
In a weil or wenn clause the whole verb moves to the end, and the particle joins it again as one word.

The finite verb of a main clause must be the second element. A fronted weil or wenn clause counts as the first, so the verb comes right after the comma and the subject follows it. The particle still splits off.
The verb ends in -t for one person and -en for die Kinder: macht / machen, singt / singen, schläft / schlafen.
explain.notes: These are called separable verbs: aufmachen, zumachen, anmachen, ausmachen. In a main clause the listener hears macht and has to wait until the last word to know whether the door is being opened or shut. The verb-second rule is why a whole clause in front pushes the subject behind the verb.
explain.fact: The Brothers Grimm, who collected Hänsel und Gretel, also began the great Deutsches Wörterbuch in 1838. It was only finished in 1961, and Jacob Grimm himself got as far as the word Frucht (fruit) before he died in 1863.
